series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/1] mm, swap: only prefer nonfull clusters on synchronous devices
series_items.patch_summary: This patch partially reverts a previous change that preferred non-full clusters over free ones for swap allocations on all devices. The new patch prefers free clusters again, except on synchronous devices like zram, where contiguity of slots doesn't matter and filling holes first keeps free clusters available for large folios. This change aims to improve performance by reducing the number of small write requests when rewriting swapped out memory.

From: Alexandre Ghiti <alex@ghiti.fr>
Subject: mm, swap: only prefer nonfull clusters on synchronous devices
Date: Mon, 09 Nov 2026 15:18:32 -0800

Commit 9a42aed48421 ("mm, swap: prefer nonfull over free clusters") made
the allocator fill nonfull clusters before taking free ones on swap
devices without discard.  Commit 3cedb745d354 ("mm: clarify the
folio_free_swap() for do_swap_page()") frees the swap slot on an exclusive
write fault.  Such faults now leave holes in formerly full clusters,
putting those clusters back on the nonfull list.  Reclaim allocates slots
one folio at a time, scattering a batch across the holes instead of
producing mergeable writes.  Later swapin can also require more read
requests.

On a mysql/sysbench workload in a 256 MiB memcg swapping to an NVMe
partition, 7.3 compared with the previous version produced 59% more device
read requests and 27% more write requests per transaction.  Throughput was
unchanged without iocost and fell 19% with iocost.

Prefer free clusters first on nonsynchronous devices, preserving
contiguous swap slots for merging I/O.  Keep nonfull-first on synchronous
devices such as zram: they do not merge I/O, and filling holes saves free
clusters for large folios.  Keep free-cluster preference on discard
devices to spread writes.

In the same workload, v2 reduced read requests per transaction by 14% and
write requests by 48% against its base kernel.  Throughput was unchanged
without iocost and improved 33% with iocost.  The RFC's batch-aware
allocator also improved this workload, but this policy needs no batch
information from reclaim.  Reverting the slot-freeing change would keep
swap space pinned under dirty pages; a proposed 50% swap-usage cutoff for
free-cluster preference was arbitrary and would stop helping as swap
filled.

The 7.0 to 7.2 kernels retained the swap slot after a write fault as a
side effect of 4b34f1d82c65 ("mm, swap: free the swap cache after folio is
mapped").  The observed regression requires both 9a42aed48421 and
3cedb745d354; stable backports should target trees containing both.

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20261105155032.240457-2-alex@ghiti.fr
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20261022145615.2184343-1-alex@ghiti.fr

Fixes: 9a42aed48421 ("mm, swap: prefer nonfull over free clusters")
Signed-off-by: Alexandre Ghiti <alex@ghiti.fr>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Suggested-by: Kairui Song <kasong@tencent.com>
Acked-by: Kairui Song <kasong@tencent.com>
Reviewed-by: Nhat Pham <nphamcs@gmail.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
---

 mm/swapfile.c |   19 +++++++++++++------
 1 file changed, 13 insertions(+), 6 deletions(-)

--- a/mm/swapfile.c~mm-swap-only-prefer-nonfull-clusters-on-synchronous-devices
+++ a/mm/swapfile.c
@@ -973,6 +973,17 @@ static bool __swap_cluster_alloc_entries
 	return true;
 }
 
+/*
+ * Prefer a new cluster over a nonfull one if the device needs discard, to
+ * spread out the writes, or if it is not synchronous, to keep the slots
+ * of a swapout batch contiguous so that its writes can be merged.
+ */
+static bool swap_prefer_free_cluster(struct swap_info_struct *si)
+{
+	return (si->flags & SWP_PAGE_DISCARD) ||
+	       !(si->flags & SWP_SYNCHRONOUS_IO);
+}
+
 /* Try use a new cluster for current CPU and allocate from it. */
 static unsigned int alloc_swap_scan_cluster(struct swap_info_struct *si,
 					    struct swap_cluster_info *ci,
@@ -1143,11 +1154,7 @@ static unsigned long cluster_alloc_swap_
 	}
 
 new_cluster:
-	/*
-	 * If the device need discard, prefer new cluster over nonfull
-	 * to spread out the writes.
-	 */
-	if (si->flags & SWP_PAGE_DISCARD) {
+	if (swap_prefer_free_cluster(si)) {
 		found = alloc_swap_scan_list(si, &si->free_clusters, folio, false);
 		if (found)
 			goto done;
@@ -1159,7 +1166,7 @@ new_cluster:
 			goto done;
 	}
 
-	if (!(si->flags & SWP_PAGE_DISCARD)) {
+	if (!swap_prefer_free_cluster(si)) {
 		found = alloc_swap_scan_list(si, &si->free_clusters, folio, false);
 		if (found)
 			goto done;

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a performance regression in the Linux kernel, specifically related to swap I/O operations on synchronous devices like NVMe partitions. The issue arises from two commits: one that prefers non-full clusters over free ones and another that frees swap slots on exclusive write faults. This leads to scattered writes and increased read requests, resulting in decreased throughput. The patch proposes a solution by only preferring non-full clusters on synchronous devices, which improves performance metrics such as device read and write requests per transaction and throughput.

version_history.subject: [PATCH v5 0/7] sched/numa: stop VMA scan filters from gating promotion

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 1/7] mm: support promotion-only NUMA hinting scans
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new NUMA hinting scan mode called 'promotion-only' that allows the kernel to focus on identifying when VMAs become active, rather than optimizing scanning activity based on heuristics like read-only VMAs or VMA activeness. The patch adds a new flag MM_CP_PROT_NUMA_PROMO_ONLY and modifies various functions in the mm module to use this flag to determine the type of walk to perform. This change is necessary for memory-tiering fixes and improves the interface by keeping it focused on scan intent, rather than plumbing VMA-derived state.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 2/7] mm: allow shared folios to be promoted to a fast tier
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows shared copy-on-write folios and executable file folios mapped by multiple processes to be promoted from slow memory to a faster tier, as long as the migration is from south to north. This change enables promotion for low-tier folios moving to top-tier, while maintaining existing restrictions for ordinary placement and non-promotion migrations. The patch also renames the `folio_use_access_time` function to `folio_numab_promotable` to better reflect its purpose.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 3/7] sched/numa: scan read-only file mappings in tiering mode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) balancing code to scan read-only file mappings when tiering is enabled, but only performs promotion scans on these mappings. This change prevents hot file folios from being placed on slow memory in tiering mode, which can cause east-west placement bouncing. The patch also updates the walk type for each VMA (Virtual Memory Area) based on the balancing-mode snapshot taken in task_numa_work().

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 4/7] sched/numa: separate VMA placement from scan continuation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the logic of VMA placement from scan continuation in the Linux kernel's NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) scheduling code. The existing `vma_is_accessed` function returns true for both placement eligibility and scan progress, which is not distinguishable by callers. This patch renames the function to `vma_needs_placement_scan`, introduces a new field in the `struct vma_numab_state` to track promotion-only scans, and updates the task's NUMA work to handle continuation state correctly. The separation allows PID-inactive VMAs to be scanned for promotion without treating scan continuation as evidence of placement eligibility.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 5/7] sched/numa: scan PID-inactive VMAs for promotion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series enhances the vma scanning logic in the Linux kernel to promote hot slow-tier memory by bypassing a filter that suppresses faults for PID-inactive VMAs. The change allows inactive VMAs to receive promotion-only scans, which helps maintain tier residency and reduces CXL bandwidth utilization.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses an issue in NUMA balancing where VMA scan filters were preventing memory-tier promotion, leading to unexpected bandwidth utilization and poor performance on certain workloads. The problem was identified when testing fairness controls and found that numa balancing was broken due to recent shmem fixes. The patches plumb the scan reasoning into the prot_none injection while retaining placement-scan filtering, allowing for correct promotion of hot memory to local nodes. The series includes several related cleanups and is designed to be backported to stable kernels.

Thanks for the review and the testing.

Agreed on the new -ENOMEM condition. It is a real behaviour change that
affects stable kernels. I will add the following to the commit message
in v3:

tasks allocating concurrently against the same memory.max may see a
spurious failure. That failure frees the folio, returns the global
reservation, and undoes the hugetlb cgroup charge, so no accounting is
left behind.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/8] nfsd: Report vetted delegated timestamps in GETATTR replies
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the NFS server where it incorrectly reports delegated timestamps to clients. The issue arises when the server receives a CB_GETATTR reply, which contains raw time_deleg_access and time_deleg_modify values that have not been vetted for validity. These values are then overridden by the server, causing incorrect timestamps to be reported to the client. This patch removes the override, ensuring that only vetted delegated timestamps are returned in GETATTR responses.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/8] nfsd: Honor delegated timestamps when change and size match
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the NFSv4 server where delegated timestamps are not honored when the change and size attributes match. The problem occurs because the holder's WRITEs do not update the mtime or change attribute on the server, causing other clients to see new data with the pre-WRITE mtime. The patch addresses this issue by always applying the CB_GETATTR times for timestamp delegations, recording applied times in the delegation structure, and marking the file modified if necessary. Additionally, it fixes issues related to atime updates and reporting of the stat-based change attribute.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/8] nfsd: don't stamp over an applied delegated mtime at DELEGRETURN
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the NFSv4 server where the mtime of a file is overwritten by the current time when a delegated write operation is completed, even if the client has already applied its own mtime. The patch ensures that the mtime is only updated if it passes the ctime check, and sets the ctime to the current time in this case. It also shares the vetting function between SETATTR and CB_GETATTR operations to prevent divergent behavior.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 4/8] nfsd: don't vet delegated times against an exclusive-create verifier
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the NFSv4 server where delegated times are not properly vetted against an exclusive-create verifier. When a client performs an exclusive create, the server stores the client's verifier in atime and mtime until the client sets real times. However, when a delegation is granted on this OPEN, the holder's times are always accepted, including times older than the file itself. The patch introduces a new function to set time floors for delegated timestamps, which uses the ctime as the floor for atime and mtime in case of an exclusive create. This ensures that the server properly rejects times equal to their floor and allows holders to replace the verifier with a time equal to the ctime.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 5/8] nfsd: mark the delegation written on COPY/CLONE instead of stamping c/mtime
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the NFSv4 server to mark a delegation as written on COPY/CLONE operations instead of updating the c/mtime attributes. This change ensures that the client's coarse timestamp does not interfere with the server's ability to update the ctime when the holder returns its times after DELEGRETURN. The patch also removes unnecessary code and updates various functions to handle this new behavior.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 6/8] fs: check a fine-grained time before clamping a delegated ctime
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a timing issue in inode_set_ctime_deleg() where the coarse time can trail an update just past a fine-grained ctime handed out in the current tick. The patch introduces a check for a fine-grained time before clamping the update, ensuring that later coarse stamps cannot land before it.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/4] mm: zswap: fix shrinker count for the root memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the zswap shrinker that causes it to incorrectly report the number of freeable entries for the root memory cgroup (memcg). The issue arises because the memcg's compression ratio is calculated from stats that do not include the root memcg's own entries. As a result, when the root memcg has no descendants with zswap entries, the shrinker reports nothing to reclaim, and its entries are never written back. To fix this, the patch uses the pool-wide counters for the root memcg instead of its stats, ensuring that all zswap entries are accounted for. This change also eliminates the need to flush the root memcg's stats, which was previously required.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/4] mm: memcg: read root lruvec stats from the node counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the way the root memory cgroup (memcg) reads its LRU vector statistics from node counters. For most stats, it directly reads from the node counter to avoid flushing the entire system, which is expensive. However, for certain kernel memory stats and hugetlb, it still needs to read the rstat value because their node counters also count unaccounted memory. This change improves accuracy of root memcg statistics and reduces flush overhead.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/4] mm: workingset: skip the root memcg flush in workingset_test_recent()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the workingset_test_recent() function to skip flushing the root memory cgroup's statistics when it is not necessary. The function now checks if the eviction memory cgroup is the root cgroup before deciding whether to flush its statistics. This optimization reduces the time taken for a root flush from 69us on an 80-CPU machine with little activity, and 0.9ms with high activity, down to negligible time. The patch also notes that flushing is still necessary for reclaim operations, but this change improves performance on systems with many memory cgroups.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 4/4] mm/damon/core: use node counters instead of flushing the root memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the DAMON core to use node counters instead of flushing the root memory cgroup (memcg) statistics when calculating LRU sizes for the goal's memcg on its node. This change improves performance by reducing the frequency of flush operations, which were previously unratelimited and occurred every time the goal was evaluated. The patch achieves this by leveraging a new function in lruvec_page_state() that directly reads the root memcg's LRU sizes from the node counters.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch set improves performance by allowing the root memory cgroup (memcg) to read global counters directly instead of flushing its stats, which is expensive and can be stale. This change affects various kernel components, including zswap, LRU sizes, workingset, rotation, and reclaim writeback counts. The patches also make adjustments for specific use cases where reading global counters isn't sufficient or would introduce additional complexity. Overall, the goal is to reduce overhead and improve accuracy of memory cgroup statistics.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch fixes an issue where migration entries in the Linux kernel are being treated as partial unmaps, leading to incorrect behavior such as unnecessary folio splits and overcounting of split_deferred statistics. patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page allocation logic to only skip nodes with active kswapd if they are also below their target watermark. This change addresses a problem where high-order requests would wake up kswapd, causing it to stay awake and allocate pages from other nodes even when there was plenty of free memory on the original node. The patch aims to prevent this thrashing by only skipping nodes that are both under kswapd's control and have insufficient memory. This change is based on observations of Meta production workloads running on 2-NUMA systems, where processes would continuously allocate pages from a preferred node despite having hundreds of GB of free memory. The patch has been tested to show improved allocation behavior, with 100% of pages being served from the preferred node after applying the fix.

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [EXT.MSG] Re: [PATCH RFC bpf-next 0/2] bpf: Do not let preemption cause false recursion drops in trampoline progs
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch addresses the issue of false recursion drops in trampoline programs caused by preemption. It introduces per-task, per-program tracking to replace the existing per-cpu recursion guard. The patch gives bpf_run_ctx a pointer to its outer ctx and associated bpf_prog, allowing it to traverse the nesting chain at trampoline entry. This approach reduces cross-task misses and improves performance, as demonstrated by test results showing a significant reduction in recursion misses.

review_comments.raw_body:
I haven't proposed moving away from an in-kernel solution. Your patch
is the same design I proposed earlier in this thread ("This is what I
have in mind for v2") with Andrii's bpf_ctx suggestion folded in, and
it's what I've been putting together for v2 (unless someone comes up
with a better direction), which is nearly ready to
post, so let's avoid duplicating the work.

tracepoints, and BPF_PROG_TEST_RUN, and disables the per-CPU private
stack for preemptible tracing progs since two tasks can now run the
same prog concurrently on one CPU.

- Passing prog to bpf_set_run_ctx() churns all callers that don't do
  recursion checks, and doesn't fit bpf_prog_run_array_sleepable(),
  which reuses one bpf_run_ctx across all progs in the array. In v2,

series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug where the Linux kernel fails to update the page cache after a write operation, leading to stale data being read from disk. series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 01/18] mm: free PG_rcu_free folios only after an RCU grace period
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new page flag, PG_rcu_free, which allows folios to be freed only after an RCU (Read-Copy Update) grace period. review_comments.author: Linus Torvalds
review_comments.summary: Linus Torvalds pointed out that RCU freeing of pages is already implemented in other areas, such as TLB shootdown, and suggested that the new PG_rcu_free flag could have been designed to be more straightforward if it had been introduced earlier. He noted that existing hacks in this area are complicated due to the complexity of architecture-specific code and would be painful to convert to a new order.
review_comments.raw_body:
So for an example of a place that already does RCU freeing of pages -
*not* folios - look at the TLB shootdown.

It's very round-about and hard to tell, but it's using

  tlb_remove_table_free
    call_rcu(&batch->rcu, tlb_remove_table_rcu);

and that then does

  tlb_remove_table_rcu ->
    __tlb_remove_table_free ->
      __tlb_remove_table ->
        pagetable_dtor_free ->
          pagetable_free ->
            __pagetable_free ->
               __free_pages(page, compound_order(page))

(and I might have messed this up - this really is a rats nest of
nested inline functions).

And in order to do this all, it sets up *another* page just to contain
the batching (which is also RCU-free'd)

Now, the batching is probably a very good thing in that context, so
I'm not actually suggesting this should be converted to some common
RCU-freeing thing.

Rather, I'm pointing out that we have existing hacks in this area that
have grown up over time and would have been a *lot* less hacky if we
had had a proper RCU-freeing page allocator back when that whole TLB
freeing code was written.

So I'm not saying "we should unify this". But I *am* saying "look, RCU
freeing of pages is _already_ a thing, and we have complicated hacky
things in place for it".

And they are complicated not because they necessarily should be
complicated, but because we solved the TLB shootdown after we already
had tons of complex architecture-specific code in place, and we
basically ended up adding that RCU phase on top of that existing
per-architecture complexity and abstraction.

*NOW* it would be actually fairly painful to try to convert the TLB
shootdown to a new order. But originally, it would have been very nice
if we had just had a "Oh, mark this page for RCU freeing".

(In all fairness, we also did it that way because some architectures
don't need the RCU delay simply because they have some other hardware
page walking infrastructure than the actual page tables the kernel
builds up. Not that those architectures *matter* today, but some of
that per-architecture inline function stuff is required to basically
isolate these kinds of decisions from the MM code - that deep inline
function indirection has a reason that is entirely independent of the
freeing side).

                    Linus

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 05/18] mm: expedite the grace period when a CPU has many deferred frees
series_items.patch_summary: This patch aims to improve the performance of deferred frees in the Linux kernel by introducing an expedited grace period when a CPU has many pending folios (memory allocations). When more than 4 MiB is pending on a CPU, the patch takes both lists and frees them after an expedited grace period. This approach ensures that memory is freed quickly when it's needed, without waiting for the normal grace period. The patch also introduces a new counter in /proc/vmstat to track the number of times this expedited process has freed memory. The goal is to prevent memory bottlenecks and improve system responsiveness, especially during bulk frees triggered by operations like file truncation or fadvise(POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED).

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 06/18] mm: free the pages waiting for a grace period before OOM
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's memory management to free pages waiting for a grace period before invoking the Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer. When reclaim fails, it checks if freeing these waiting pages and what reclaim can still free would bring an eligible zone above its minimum watermark. If so, it drains these pages straight to the buddy lists, allowing the OOM killer to be invoked only when necessary. This approach is designed to reduce the likelihood of invoking the OOM killer unnecessarily, which can lead to system instability.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 07/18] mm: free the pages waiting for a grace period before isolation fails
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where migration of pages to a new zone fails due to pages waiting for a grace period after being freed. The patch introduces a new function, `rcu_free_sync()`, which frees all waiting folios and their associated work. This allows the allocation process to proceed without failing due to pending page migrations. The change is made in two key functions: `offline_pages()` and `alloc_contig_range()`. In `offline_pages()`, if a migration pass has occurred and there are pages waiting for a grace period, the function calls `rcu_free_sync()` before retrying the allocation. Similarly, in `alloc_contig_range()`, if the check for isolated pages fails due to pending migrations, the function frees any waiting folios before attempting to allocate memory again.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 08/18] mm/compaction: free the migrated folios that wait for a grace period
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue in the Linux kernel's compaction mechanism, where migrated folios that wait for a grace period can cause compaction to fail more often. The problem arises when a block is migrated and its folios are not immediately freed, causing subsequent migrations to occur unnecessarily. To resolve this, the patch introduces a new function `rcu_free_drain()` that frees these waiting folios before draining the per-cpu lists. This change improves compaction efficiency and reduces allocation stalls in defrag_mode.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 09/18] mm/memory-failure: handle folios with PG_rcu_free
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where memory_failure() and soft_offline_page() cannot handle pages that are waiting for an RCU (Read-Copy-Update) grace period, which causes them to be ignored or handled incorrectly. The patch introduces a new function mf_free_rcu_pages() that frees these pages before attempting to access them, ensuring they are properly handled by memory_failure(). Additionally, it modifies the get_any_page() and memory_failure() functions to wait for an RCU grace period after setting PG_hwpoison on a page, allowing readers to safely unmap the poisoned page. This patch aims to improve the handling of pages waiting for an RCU grace period in the Linux kernel's memory failure mechanism.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 10/18] mm: have folio_mark_accessed() return whether the folio is hot
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the `folio_mark_accessed` function to return a boolean value indicating whether the accessed folio is considered 'hot'. A hot folio is one that is either unevictable or has its access flags set. This change prepares for reading the status of folios without requiring an explicit reference to them. The patch updates the `folio_mark_accessed` function and related code in the Linux kernel's memory management (mm) module.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 11/18] mm/filemap: mark a folio accessed in one place in filemap_read()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch simplifies the filemap_read() function by moving the folio access marking into a single helper function, filemap_read_accessed(). This function is called once per folio in the loop, eliminating duplicate code and making it easier to decide which folios are worth reading without a reference. The change does not affect the behavior of the function, but prepares for future improvements.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 12/18] mm/filemap: set PG_rcu_free on the folios that reads keep coming back to
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new flag, PG_rcu_free, which allows the kernel to delay freeing memory associated with a folio that is frequently accessed by readers. The flag is set in filemap_read() when a folio is found to be hot based on LRU records or previous read access patterns. This approach aims to balance the trade-off between delaying free of streaming reads and truncating files, while also avoiding unnecessary delays for cold data. The patch includes changes to various kernel files to support this new flag and provide statistics on its usage.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 13/18] mm/filemap: read from the page cache without folio references
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the page cache read performance by allowing reads to occur without taking a reference on the folio, reducing the bounce of refcounts between CPUs. It achieves this by copying data from folios that are about to be freed under RCU read lock and using a batch size of up to 512 KiB per section. The patch also optimizes large folios and introduces checks for poisoned pages, uptodate status, and other conditions that require the slow path. This approach aims to reduce overhead and improve performance in scenarios with multiple CPUs accessing the same file.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 14/18] mm/filemap: read large folios without folio references
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's filemap module to allow reading large folios without creating a reference to them. A large folio is one that spans all or none of its range, and once the last page in its range is reached, subsequent pages can be copied from the same folio. The patch introduces a new function `filemap_read_rcu_size` to calculate how much data can be copied from a folio without creating a reference. It also updates the `filemap_read_rcu_lookup` function to handle large folios and split them correctly when necessary. This change aims to improve performance by reducing the number of references created during file I/O operations.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 15/18] mm/filemap: don't store f_ra.prev_pos for FMODE_RANDOM files
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the filemap_read function to skip storing f_ra.prev_pos for files that have FMODE_RANDOM set, which is used by applications like RocksDB to read files at random offsets from multiple threads. The patch addresses a performance issue where reads were slower due to unnecessary shared store operations. It keeps the slow path of the function intact and only skips the store operation when filemap_read_rcu has already done a full read without folio references.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 16/18] mm/shmem: count accesses to a folio the way filemap_read() does
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the way accesses to a folio in tmpfs are counted. Instead of only marking a folio as accessed when a read starts at its beginning, it marks the folio accessed unless the previous read through the file ended in the same position. This change ensures that reads that start anywhere within a folio count towards its access age, rather than just those that start at the beginning. Additionally, this patch sets PG_rcu_free on tmpfs folios that are repeatedly accessed.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 17/18] mm/shmem: read without folio references
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the shmem_file_read_iter function to take a reference on every folio it reads, which can cause small reads of one tmpfs file from many CPUs to bounce the folio's refcount. To fix this issue, the patch introduces a new function called filemap_read_rcu that copies data from the page cache without taking any references. This function is used in place of shmem_file_read_iter for small reads, allowing multiple CPUs to read from the same tmpfs file simultaneously without causing reference count bounces.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 18/18] mm/filemap: add a debugfs switch for lockless page cache reads
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a debugfs switch to control lockless page cache reads in the Linux kernel. The goal is to provide a way to turn off lockless reads, which can be problematic for certain workloads or when there's a bug in the read path. The switch is added as a static key that can be enabled or disabled through debugfs. When enabled, it stops filemap_read() and shmem_file_read_iter() from setting PG_rcu_free and copying without a reference. This allows users to test and verify the correctness of lockless reads before they are enabled by default.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series proposes a change to how Linux handles page cache reads, allowing multiple CPUs to read from the same folio without taking a reference. This is done by introducing a new flag PG_rcu_free and deferring the freeing of folios until an RCU grace period. The goal is to reduce contention between readers and improve performance in scenarios where many threads are reading the same pages. The patch series includes 18 patches that implement this change, including modifications to filemap_read(), shmem, and other related functions.

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about memory safety when reading from the page cache without taking a reference, explaining that adding PG_rcu_free flag would allow readers to safely access folios marked for deferred free during an RCU grace period.
review_comments.raw_body:
From: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Reading a page cache folio without taking a reference would keep CPUs
that read the same file from bouncing its refcount.  But without a
reference the folio can be freed, and its memory reused, while the
reader copies from it.

Add PG_rcu_free: the free of a folio with the flag waits for an RCU
grace period.  A reader that saw the flag under rcu_read_lock(), and
then still found the folio where it looked, can read it until
rcu_read_unlock().  A split copies the flag, as such a reader may still
be reading the new folios.

The folios wait on per-CPU lists, one grace period in flight per CPU:
call_rcu() per folio would queue a callback for every folio of a
truncated file.  A work, which can reschedule, frees each batch.
Reclaim depends on these frees, so the workqueue is WQ_MEM_RECLAIM.

The flag is 64-bit only (CONFIG_PAGE_RCU_FREE): page flags are scarce
on 32-bit, and the contention this avoids is a problem of large
machines.  It is off on PREEMPT_RT, where expedited grace periods are
normal ones, so the waiting pages cannot be freed quickly when memory
runs short.

pgfree_rcu in /proc/vmstat counts the deferred pages.  Nothing sets the
flag yet.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

+++ b/include/linux/page-flags.h
@@ -111,6 +111,9 @@ enum pageflags {
 	PG_swapbacked,		/* Page is backed by RAM/swap */
 	PG_unevictable,		/* Page is "unevictable"  */

 #endif /* CONFIG_MEM_ALLOC_PROFILING */
 
+/*
+ * Each CPU has at most one grace period in flight (@queued), covering
+ * @batch.  Folios freed meanwhile wait on @pending for the next one.
+ */
+struct rcu_free_pcpu {
+	spinlock_t lock;
+	bool queued;
+	struct list_head pending;
+	struct list_head batch;
+	struct rcu_work rwork;
+};
+
+static DEFINE_PER_CPU(struct rcu_free_pcpu, rcu_free_pcpu);
+
+static struct workqueue_struct *rcu_free_wq __ro_after_init;
+
+static void rcu_free_start(struct rcu_free_pcpu *r)
+{
+	lockdep_assert_held(&r->lock);
+
+	if (r->queued || list_empty(&r->pending))
+		return;
+
+	list_splice_init(&r->pending, &r->batch);
+	r->queued = true;
+	WARN_ON_ONCE(!queue_rcu_work(rcu_free_wq, &r->rwork));
+}
+
+static void rcu_free_pages(struct list_head *list)
+{
+	struct folio_batch fbatch;
+	struct folio *folio, *next;
+
+	folio_batch_init(&fbatch);
+	list_for_each_entry_safe(folio, next, list, lru) {
+		if (!folio_batch_add(&fbatch, folio)) {
+			free_unref_folios(&fbatch);
+			cond_resched_tasks_rcu_qs();
+		}
+	}
+	if (folio_batch_count(&fbatch))
+		free_unref_folios(&fbatch);
+}
+
+static void rcu_free_workfn(struct work_struct *work)
+{
+	struct rcu_free_pcpu *r = container_of(to_rcu_work(work),
+					       struct rcu_free_pcpu, rwork);
+	LIST_HEAD(done);
+
+	spin_lock_irq(&r->lock);
+	list_splice_init(&r->batch, &done);
+	r->queued = false;
+	rcu_free_start(r);
+	spin_unlock_irq(&r->lock);
+
+	rcu_free_pages(&done);
+}
+
+static void rcu_free_defer(struct folio *folio)
+{
+	struct rcu_free_pcpu *r = raw_cpu_ptr(&rcu_free_pcpu);
+	unsigned long flags;
+
+	spin_lock_irqsave(&r->lock, flags);
+	list_add_tail(&folio->lru, &r->pending);
+	rcu_free_start(r);
+	spin_unlock_irqrestore(&r->lock, flags);
+}
+
+static void __init rcu_free_init(void)
+{
+	int cpu;
+
+	if (!IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_PAGE_RCU_FREE))
+		return;
+
+	rcu_free_wq = alloc_workqueue("rcu_free",
+				      WQ_MEM_RECLAIM | WQ_PERCPU, 0);
+
+	for_each_possible_cpu(cpu) {
+		struct rcu_free_pcpu *r = per_cpu_ptr(&rcu_free_pcpu, cpu);
+
+		spin_lock_init(&r->lock);
+		INIT_LIST_HEAD(&r->pending);
+		INIT_LIST_HEAD(&r->batch);
+		INIT_RCU_WORK(&r->rwork, rcu_free_workfn);
+	}
+}

From: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

PG_rcu_free holds back the reuse of a folio's memory until a grace
period after the folio is freed.  A stolen page cache pipe buffer is
reused without being freed: remove_mapping() takes the folio out of the
page cache and the caller keeps it.  fuse_try_move_folio() puts it into
a fuse file, where writes change it under a reader that found it before
the steal.

Drop ->try_steal from page_cache_pipe_buf_ops.  fuse_try_move_folio()
and virtio_console's pipe_to_sg() then copy, as they already do when
stealing fails.  SPLICE_F_MOVE from the page cache into a fuse file or
a virtio console now copies.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
[kas: rewrote the changelog]
Signed-off-by: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org>

fuse_try_move_folio() takes the folio of a pipe buffer and puts it into
a fuse file, where writes change it.  A folio with PG_rcu_free may still
be copied by a lockless page cache read that found it before it left
the page cache.

Such a folio reaches fuse when a mapped file page is gifted with
vmsplice(SPLICE_F_GIFT) and its file is then truncated.
fuse_check_folio() refuses it only because the flag is not among those
it allows, and with a dump_page().

Copy such a folio instead, as fuse does whenever it cannot take one.

Signed-off-by: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org>

+	/* A lockless page cache read may still be copying from it */

+		goto out_fallback_unlock;

 	folio_clear_uptodate(newfolio);
 	folio_clear_mappedtodisk(newfolio);

Deferred folios have refcount 0 and are not on the free lists, so no
counter shows them.  Memory that waits for a grace period is missing
from the free count and from every LRU count.

Count it per zone in NR_FREE_RCU_PAGES: nr_free_rcu in /proc/vmstat,
free_rcu in show_free_areas().  Preparation for freeing the waiting
pages sooner when they hold back memory that is needed.

review_comments.raw_body:
A page whose free waits for an RCU grace period has refcount 0 and is
neither on the LRU nor in the buddy allocator.  memory_failure() and
soft_offline_page() cannot handle such a page: get_any_page() retries a
few times and gives up.  Soft offline of the page fails, and a hard
error is ignored.  If the page is part of a large folio, the folio is
later freed with the poisoned page in it, and that page can be handed
out again.

Free the waiting pages first when the page looks like one of them, and
again on each retry in get_any_page(): the page can be freed while it
retries.  memory_failure() has to do it before it sets PG_hwpoison.  The
free of a poisoned order-0 page drops the page instead of returning it
to the buddy allocator, so a later drain would still leave the error
ignored.

A folio with PG_rcu_free that is still in use may be copied by a reader
that holds no reference.  When memory_failure() succeeds, its caller can
unmap the page from the direct map under such a reader.  Wait for a
grace period before returning success.  By then the page has left the
page cache, or is an order-0 folio with PG_hwpoison, which a reader that
starts after the grace period has to check.

Wait at the end, not right after setting PG_hwpoison.  A large folio is
split later, and until the new folios are in the page cache, a reader
can still copy the poisoned page as part of the large one.

Both callers hold mf_mutex and can wait for the grace period.

Trying to make it specific to one special freeing path only makes it
fragile and less obvious, and results in anybody who then uses some
other freeing model to miss the RCU thing.

It also means that suddenly nobody else can use the RCU path for their own uses.

lock-free area of the kernel wants RCU freeing.

On Mon, 9 Nov 2026 at 09:24, David Hildenbrand (Arm) <david@kernel.org> wrote:
> >
> > I think trying to corral it into some special case is the last thing
> > we want to do. It only makes things less potentially useful and more
> > fragile.
> Let me wrap my head around how this would look when we decouple pages from
> folios, where pages might not have a ->lru anymore, or not even a refcount.

So for an example of a place that already does RCU freeing of pages -
*not* folios - look at the TLB shootdown.

It's very round-about and hard to tell, but it's using

  tlb_remove_table_free
    call_rcu(&batch->rcu, tlb_remove_table_rcu);

and that then does

  tlb_remove_table_rcu ->
    __tlb_remove_table_free ->
      __tlb_remove_table ->
        pagetable_dtor_free ->
          pagetable_free ->
            __pagetable_free ->
               __free_pages(page, compound_order(page))

(and I might have messed this up - this really is a rats nest of
nested inline functions).

And in order to do this all, it sets up *another* page just to contain
the batching (which is also RCU-free'd)

Now, the batching is probably a very good thing in that context, so
I'm not actually suggesting this should be converted to some common
RCU-freeing thing.

Rather, I'm pointing out that we have existing hacks in this area that
have grown up over time and would have been a *lot* less hacky if we
had had a proper RCU-freeing page allocator back when that whole TLB
freeing code was written.

So I'm not saying "we should unify this". But I *am* saying "look, RCU
freeing of pages is _already_ a thing, and we have complicated hacky
things in place for it".

And they are complicated not because they necessarily should be
complicated, but because we solved the TLB shootdown after we already
had tons of complex architecture-specific code in place, and we
basically ended up adding that RCU phase on top of that existing
per-architecture complexity and abstraction.

*NOW* it would be actually fairly painful to try to convert the TLB
shootdown to a new order. But originally, it would have been very nice
if we had just had a "Oh, mark this page for RCU freeing".

(In all fairness, we also did it that way because some architectures
don't need the RCU delay simply because they have some other hardware
page walking infrastructure than the actual page tables the kernel
builds up. Not that those architectures *matter* today, but some of
that per-architecture inline function stuff is required to basically
isolate these kinds of decisions from the MM code - that deep inline
function indirection has a reason that is entirely independent of the
freeing side).

review_comments.raw_body:
On Tue, 10 Nov 2026 16:25:54 +0000
Kiryl Shutsemau <kas@kernel.org> wrote:

> On Wed, Nov 04, 2026 at 02:28:06PM -0800, Usama Arif wrote:
> > +#ifdef CONFIG_MITIGATION_ITS
> > +	/*
> > +	 * Returns are patched before alternatives. Align the replacement
> > +	 * source so its return is in the first half of a cache line and ITS
> > +	 * retains its thunk. The copied return can then execute in either
> > +	 * half of a cache line.
> > +	 */
> > +	.pushsection .altinstr_replacement, "ax"
> > +	.balign 64
> > +	.popsection
> > +#endif
> > +	ALTERNATIVE __stringify(cmpq $0x20, %rcx; jb .Lhandle_tail), \
> > +		    __stringify(rep movsb; RET), X86_FEATURE_FSRM  
> 
> Does this mean any RET in a replacement needs the same alignment? Would
> anything catch it if the next one doesn't have it?

My suspicion is that ideally 'yes'.
But someone said (in this thread) that it is worse for RET in the first
half a cache line - so aligning the replacement that way is better.)

> Linus' layout keeps the RET out of the replacement, with no padding:
> 
> 	movq %rdi, %rax
> 	movq %rdx, %rcx
> 	ALTERNATIVE "jmp memcpy_orig", "rep movsb", X86_FEATURE_FSRM
> 	RET
> 
> Non-FSRM takes the same jump it takes today. Does that avoid the ITS
> problem? Why not this layout?

It adds a jump to the non-FSRM path.
Cold cache that is likely to be measurable.
(But not if RET ends up being anything other than 0xc3 -  that will
just kill everything.)

> 
> > +	/*
> > +	 * RCX holds the count for REP MOVSB and scalar copying; RDX is scratch.
> > +	 * Shift RDX to check length >= 2048 without destroying the REP count.
> > +	 * The 10-byte alternative fits a NOP without ERMS.
> > +	 */
> > +	ALTERNATIVE "", __stringify(shrq $11, %rdx; jnz .Lerms), X86_FEATURE_ERMS  
> 
> The RCX/RDX swap is most of the diff, and all it saves is one MOV on
> copies of 2K and up.

Register-register moves don't cost much (they can even be done my the
register renaming logic rather than the alu - but still have to be
fetched and decoded), but needing them is a bit of 'lack of attention
detail' when a simple backtrack can get the value where it is needed.
gcc is very bad at it, a compiler really ought to do a lot better.

David

> 
> What about something like this? Untested.
> 
> diff --git a/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S b/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S
> --- a/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S
> +++ b/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S
> @@ -31,11 +31,9 @@
>   * which the compiler could/should do much better anyway.
>   */
>  SYM_TYPED_FUNC_START(__memcpy)
> -	ALTERNATIVE "jmp memcpy_orig", "", X86_FEATURE_FSRM
> -
>  	movq %rdi, %rax
>  	movq %rdx, %rcx
> -	rep movsb
> +	ALTERNATIVE "jmp memcpy_orig", "rep movsb", X86_FEATURE_FSRM
>  	RET
>  SYM_FUNC_END(__memcpy)
>  EXPORT_SYMBOL(__memcpy)
> @@ -45,11 +43,11 @@ SYM_PIC_ALIAS(memcpy)
>  EXPORT_SYMBOL(memcpy)
> 
>  SYM_FUNC_START_LOCAL(memcpy_orig)
> -	movq %rdi, %rax
> -
>  	cmpq $0x20, %rdx
>  	jb .Lhandle_tail
> 
> +	ALTERNATIVE "", __stringify(shrq $11, %rcx; jnz .Lerms), X86_FEATURE_ERMS
> +
>  	/*
>  	 * We check whether memory false dependence could occur,
>  	 * then jump to corresponding copy mode.
> @@ -169,5 +167,10 @@ SYM_FUNC_START_LOCAL(memcpy_orig)
> 
>  .Lend:
>  	RET
> +
> +.Lerms:
> +	movq %rdx, %rcx
> +	rep movsb
> +	RET
>  SYM_FUNC_END(memcpy_orig)
>

>>> PG_head is written before clear_compound_page(), after which new_head

>> read new_folio->flags.f?

> It is not. The comment names the wrong word: PG_waiters can be set
> concurrently on the old head, not on new_folio.

Yes, thank you for the explanation. I confused myself when writing
the comment. At this code place, before clear_compound_head(),
reference-less accessors can only see the old folio.

>
> CPU1 and CPU2 below are two faults on a migration entry that points at
> new_head. Both take this path:
>
>   do_swap_page()
>     migration_entry_wait()
>       softleaf_entry_wait_on_locked()
>         softleaf_to_folio()
>           page_folio()           <-- old head or new_head?

>           set_bit(PG_waiters)    <-- on that folio's flags

>
> CPU0: __split_folio_to_order()  CPU1: fault           CPU2: fault
>
>                                 1. page_folio()
>                                    -> old head
> 2. flags  = new_folio->flags.f
>    flags |= folio->flags.f
>                                 3. set_bit(PG_waiters)
>                                    -> folio->flags.f
> 4. new_folio->flags.f =
>            flags | PG_head
>    smp_wmb()
> 5. clear_compound_head()
>                                                       6. page_folio()
>                                                          -> new_head
>                                                       7. set_bit(PG_waiters)
>                                                          -> new_folio->flags.f
>
> 2 and 3 race on the old head's flags word.

>

>

I will clean this up and send v4. Sorry for the confusion.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/3] mm: vmscan: allow writeout of swapcache folios without anon mappings
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows the writeout of swapcache folios without anonymous mappings, enabling reclaim to write out dirty pages in swapcache even if they don't have an anonymous mapping. This is necessary because pageout() previously rejected these pages before they could be written out using the existing swap writeout path. The change affects how the filesystem checks for valid mappings and allows swapcache folios to bypass certain checks.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm/swap: publish cluster tables after reacquiring allocator locks
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a memory leak issue in the Linux kernel's swap cluster allocation mechanism. When under memory pressure, the `swap_cluster_populate()` function can publish a table while dropping its locks for a sleeping allocation. A cached allocator can consume and free this table before the populating allocator resumes, leaving the resumed scan with a NULL table. The patch ensures that the count table, cgroup table, and zero bitmap are kept private until `swap_cluster_alloc_table()` restores all allocator locks. It also installs them under the cluster lock and retains it through the scan to prevent premature freeing of these tables.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/3] mm/swap: skip relocation of tableless clusters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents a stale reclaimer from freeing a tableless swap cluster while an allocator is still populating its table. This occurs when the allocator drops its locks to populate the table, allowing the reclaimer to reach the relocation code and potentially dereference NULL in the DEBUG_VM empty check. The patch adds a check to skip relocation of tableless clusters, leaving them for the allocator under the cluster's lock. This prevents a FREE-to-NONE state cycle and ensures that the table population is completed before the cluster is freed.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses issues in the Linux kernel's swap cache and cluster table management, specifically preventing races between writeout of swapcache folios without anonymous mappings and publication of cluster tables while allocator locks are held. The patches also prevent relocation of tableless clusters, ensuring consistency in memory allocation. The changes were made to address bugs found in previous versions of the swap code.

This is particularly useful on systems that already reserve large amounts of memory with hugetlb_cma=, as it enables the crash kernel to use this existing memory as part of its working set. The goal is to keep these THPs mapped across a swap round-trip, which requires modifying the behavior of the PG_anon_exclusive flag in the presence of swap PMDs. The patch introduces new helpers for setting and clearing the _PAGE_SWP_EXCLUSIVE bit in PMD values.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 04/32] powerpc: mm: add PMD swap-exclusive helpers

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 07/32] x86: mm: add PMD swap-exclusive helpers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds helper functions for managing swap-exclusive PMDs (Page Map Entries) on x86 architectures. The goal is to allow a PMD-mapped anonymous huge page to remain mapped across a swap round-trip, which requires the PG_anon_exclusive flag to survive in a swap PMD. The new helpers reuse an existing bit in the swap PMD layout and assert that it does not alias with another reserved bit on 32-bit x86 architectures.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 08/32] mm: recognize PMD swap entries in the softleaf layer
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows the Linux kernel to recognize and handle PMD (Page Map Directory) swap entries in the softleaf layer, which is responsible for decoding non-present PMDs. The patch adds a new function `pmd_is_swap_entry()` to check if a PMD entry encodes an actual swap entry, and modifies existing functions to correctly handle swap entries. This change prepares the kernel for installing swap entries directly into PMDs, rather than first splitting them into PTE-level swap entries.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 09/32] mm/debug_vm_pgtable: test PMD swap-exclusive helpers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a test to the Linux kernel's mm/debug_vm_pgtable module to verify that PMD (Page Map Directory) swap-exclusive helpers are working correctly. The test checks for various scenarios, including setting and clearing the exclusive bit, checking for soft-dirty state, and verifying that the PMD is non-present when swap soft-dirty is set. This patch addresses a potential issue where an architecture with a PMD exclusive bit overlapping the swap type or offset field might only be caught by data corruption at runtime. The test is enabled only if the CONFIG_ARCH_HAS_PMD_SOFTLEAVES configuration option is set, indicating that the underlying architecture supports PMD soft-leaves.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 10/32] mm/migrate_device: avoid leaking folio references during THP splitting
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the Linux kernel's migration device code where an extra folio reference is taken during transparent huge page (THP) splitting, leading to a leak when the PMD is split into PTE migration entries. The fix involves removing the extra folio_get() call and using the existing migration PMD lock to prevent concurrent MADV_DONTNEED operations from clearing the PMD.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 11/32] mm: make PMD migration-entry splitting explicit
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the PMD migration-entry splitting logic in the Linux kernel to make it more explicit and easier to understand. The 'freeze' boolean parameter in functions like __split_huge_pmd() is renamed to 'to_migration_entries', which indicates that it controls whether PTE migration entries are created instead of regular PTE mappings. A new function, split_pmd_to_migration_entries(), is introduced for the only caller that wants this behavior, and assertions are added to ensure that only present or device-private PMDs are handled by __split_huge_pmd_locked(). The patch aims to improve code clarity without introducing any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 12/32] mm: split PMD swap entries into PTE swap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch splits PMD swap entries into PTE swap entries in the Linux kernel's memory management (mm) module. The goal is to ensure that when a PMD can hold a swap entry, it can also be split by various operations such as mprotect(), munmap(), or MADV_FREE. This change allows for more efficient handling of swap entries and prevents potential issues with pmdp_invalidate() and pmd_page(). The patch modifies the __split_huge_pmd_locked() function in huge_memory.c to handle PMD swap entries correctly, including updating the PTEs and removing any unnecessary reference counting.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 13/32] mm/swap: allow duplicating a range of swap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows duplicating a range of swap entries in the Linux kernel, rather than one at a time. This is necessary because some operations, such as PMD swap entry forks, require multiple slots to be duplicated simultaneously. The patch introduces new functions `swap_dup_entries_direct` and `swap_retry_table_alloc_nr` that take an additional argument for the number of entries to duplicate or allocate. It also adds inline wrappers for existing single-slot functions to maintain backwards compatibility. The range of entries must sit within a single cluster, and crossing ranges are rejected with an error code. No functional changes are intended by this patch.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 14/32] mm: handle PMD swap entries in fork path
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where PMD swap entries are not handled correctly in the fork path, leading to duplicated and unreferenced slots. The patch modifies the copy_huge_pmd function to duplicate PMD swap entries by creating new references to the source slots, clearing the exclusive marker on the source entry, and updating the mm counter accordingly. It also adds error handling for GFP_ATOMIC allocation failures in the fork path.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 15/32] mm: swap: share swap-cache allocation error cleanup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the error handling in swap-cache allocation to share a common cleanup path, simplifying code and reducing duplication.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 16/32] mm: zswap: reject high-order swap cache allocations backed by zswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch rejects high-order swap cache allocations when zswap is enabled, preventing potential issues with stale or zero data being read from disk.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 17/32] mm: swap in PMD swap entries as whole THPs during swapoff
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the swapoff process by allowing PMD swap entries to be handled as whole THPs (Transparent Huge Pages) instead of individual PTEs (Page Table Entries). This is achieved through a new function, `swap_pmd_cache_lookup`, which classifies the covered range as empty, one PMD-sized folio, or already split. The patch also introduces a new function, `unuse_pmd`, to map the first two cases back in as one THP, preserving soft-dirty, exclusive and UFFD state. If the cache is split, per-page zswap state, allocation failure, or poisoning occurs, the patch falls back to handling PTEs. The changes aim to optimize the swapoff process by reducing the number of faults required.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 18/32] fs/proc: account PMD swap entries in smaps
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the Linux kernel's /proc filesystem to correctly account for PMD swap entries in the smaps output. It introduces a new function, smaps_account_swap(), which is called when a swapped-out THP (Transparent Huge Page) is encountered. This function calculates the swap and swap PSS (Proportional Set Size) values based on the number of slots in the PMD entry. The patch also updates the smaps_pte_entry() and smaps_pmd_entry() functions to use this new function when encountering swapped-out THPs. This change ensures that swapped-out THPs are not included in AnonHugePages or Rss, and allows for accurate accounting of swap and swap PSS values.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 19/32] mm: handle soft-dirty and uffd-wp on PMD swap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the handling of soft-dirty and uffd-wp flags in PMD swap entries to ensure they are correctly updated during migration and other operations. The changes involve adding checks for PMD swap entries in various functions that manipulate these flags, ensuring that they are treated similarly to migration entries. This fixes issues where clearing soft-dirty could skip swapped-out THPs, UFFDIO_WRITEPROTECT did not arm the flag, and mremap did not mark the destination correctly.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 20/32] mm/hmm: fault PMD swap entries on demand
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the handling of absent PMD entries in the Linux kernel's Heterogeneous Memory Management (HMM) module. Specifically, it treats swapped-out huge pages as non-resident memory rather than a permanent failure, similar to how PTE swap entries are handled. This change is made by adding a check for swap entries and returning them as not valid when no fault was requested.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 21/32] mm: free PMD swap entries in zap_huge_pmd()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the zap_huge_pmd() function to handle PMD swap entries before attempting to access a folio, preventing potential memory leaks and warnings. It checks if the PMD is a swap entry, and if so, it frees the associated swap slots and updates the memory management counters accordingly.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 22/32] mm/madvise: free PMD swap entries with MADV_FREE
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the MADV_FREE behavior in Linux to free PMD swap entries when the advice covers the whole PMD, rather than only freeing individual PTEs. This change ensures that userspace gets the expected result from MADV_FREE over a swapped-out THP. The patch also moves the zap_deposited_table function above its new caller and makes no other changes to it.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 23/32] mm/madvise: skip PMD swap entries for MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of PMD swap entries in the Linux kernel's madvise function, specifically for MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT operations. It skips over swapped-out THPs (Transparent Huge Pages) that have no resident folio to deactivate or reclaim, avoiding unnecessary work and potential warnings. The approach taken is to add a check for PMD swap entries at the beginning of the madvise_cold_or_pageout_pte_range function, allowing it to return immediately if such an entry is found.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 24/32] mm/madvise: keep PMD swap entries whole for MADV_GUARD_INSTALL/REMOVE
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the MADV_GUARD_INSTALL/REMOVE callbacks in the Linux kernel to treat PMD swap entries as whole, rather than splitting them. This change ensures that these operations do not attempt to split a swapped-out huge page, which would demote it before attempting to remove the guard pages. The patch addresses an issue where the existing code was incorrectly handling PMD swap entries and causing unnecessary work.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 25/32] mm/mincore: report PMD swap-cache residency
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the mincore function where it incorrectly reports pages as resident when they are actually swapped out. The patch introduces a new function, mincore_pmd_swap, which checks if a PMD swap entry is present and returns residency information accordingly. If the PMD swap entry is huge, it directly returns residency information for all pages covered by the folio. Otherwise, it falls back to checking each individual slot as before. This patch also adds a new function, mincore_pmd_swap, which handles PMD swap entries in the absence of CONFIG_THP_SWAP. The patch aims to improve the accuracy of mincore's reporting and prevent unnecessary page faults.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 26/32] mm/khugepaged: treat PMD swap entries as mapped THPs
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged code to treat PMD swap entries as mapped THPs, allowing them to be handled similarly to present huge PMDs. This change affects how MADV_COLLAPSE behaves when encountering swapped-out THPs, ensuring that they are correctly collapsed and made resident on demand. The approach taken involves modifying the check_pmd_state function to return SCAN_PMD_MAPPED for PMD swap entries, enabling khugepaged to manage these ranges more efficiently.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 27/32] mm: handle PMD swap entries in MADV_WILLNEED
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves handling of PMD swap entries in MADV_WILLNEED operations by prefetching the whole range as one PMD-order folio instead of walking PTEs individually. This approach avoids issues with order-0 readahead and faults that follow, and also considers changes to the THP policy since the range was swapped out. The patch introduces a new function `swapin_pmd_swap_entry` that handles this scenario and allows for fallback to PTEs in case of errors or split cache configurations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 28/32] mm: handle PMD swap entries in UFFDIO_MOVE
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for moving PMD-level swap entries in UFFDIO_MOVE operations. It introduces a new function, move_swap_pmd(), which moves the entry under both PMD locks and propagates soft-dirty flags. The function also handles revalidation of cached folios and anchors their anon rmap to the destination VMA. Additionally, it rejects PMD swap entries at the destination with -EEXIST. This patch addresses an issue where aligned UFFDIO_MOVE operations over swapped-out THPs fail due to missing support for PMD-level swap entries.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 29/32] mm: don't PTE-batch a swap-in over a hardware-poisoned subpage
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents a swap-in operation from being batched over a hardware-poisoned subpage in the Linux kernel. The problem it solves is that the existing batching path does not check for poisoned subpages, allowing a potentially faulty page to be mapped and causing issues. To address this, the patch checks each subpage individually before mapping the rest of the folio, ensuring that any poisoned pages are properly reported and handled.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 30/32] mm: handle PMD swap entry faults on swap-in
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a problem where PMD swap entries would fault indefinitely due to the kernel's handling of non-present PMDs as device-private or migration entries. The patch introduces a new function `do_huge_pmd_swap_page` that resolves the whole mapping in one go, mirroring the behavior of `do_swap_page` at PMD granularity. It also adds logic to split the PMD entry and return 0 if the cache has been split, a slot is in zswap, or other conditions are met. Additionally, it refactors code to drop the folio from the swap cache under certain conditions, refuses to map folios with poisoned subpages, and calls `wp_huge_pmd` when necessary to handle write faults.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 31/32] mm: install PMD swap entries on swap-out
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the handling of PMD-mapped anonymous huge pages (THPs) during swap-out operations. When a THP is swapped out, it currently splits into smaller mappings, which can lead to performance issues and increased memory usage. This patch introduces a new approach where a single PMD-level swap entry is created for each contiguous run of slots in the swap cache, eliminating the need for splitting and reducing the number of small mappings. The patch also updates various kernel components, including huge_memory.c, rmap.c, vmscan.c, and vmstat.c, to support this new approach.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v9 32/32] selftests/mm: add PMD swap entry tests
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a set of tests to verify the behavior of PMD (Page Map Directory) swap entries in the Linux kernel. The tests cover various scenarios, including swapping out and back in THPs (Transparent Huge Pages), fork and cow operations, write and read access, and other edge cases. The tests use the MADV_PAGEOUT flag to swap out pages and verify that the thp_swpout_pmd counter is incremented correctly. Additionally, the patch adds a /proc/vmstat field reader to allow other tests to access this information. The tests are designed to be run on both synchronous and asynchronous devices, and skip certain operations if the kernel does not support them. With zswap enabled, some tests skip PMD-restoration assertions due to legitimate fallback behavior.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces PMD-level swap entries for anonymous Trans Huge Pages (THPs). The goal is to allow a PMD-mapped THP to be kept mapped across a swap round-trip, which requires modifications to the LoongArch architecture. The approach taken involves adding helpers to manage the exclusive bit in PMDs, enabling the survival of PG_anon_exclusive in swap PMDs.

review_comments.author: Usama Arif (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about PMD swap entries being split into PTE-level swap entries during reclaim, explaining that the series introduces a PMD-level swap entry to preserve the huge mapping across the swap round-trip and reduce page-table overhead. The author confirmed that this is the intended behavior and that the patch will proceed with the current implementation.
review_comments.raw_body:
When reclaim swaps out a PMD-mapped anonymous THP today, the PMD is
split into HPAGE_PMD_NR PTE-level swap entries via TTU_SPLIT_HUGE_PMD
before unmap. This series introduces a PMD-level swap entry so the
huge mapping can survive the swap round-trip and do_huge_pmd_swap_page()
can restore the PMD mapping directly on swap-in, without waiting for
khugepaged to collapse the range later.

The PMD swap entry is a compact page-table encoding for HPAGE_PMD_NR
consecutive swap slots. swap_map accounting remains per-slot and is
unchanged. A PMD swap entry does not promise that the swap cache always
contains one PMD-sized folio. While the cache is empty or contains one
PMD-sized folio, PMD-level handling can proceed. Once the cache has
split/per-slot state, users either inspect the individual slots directly
(mincore) or split the PMD swap entry and retry through the PTE path
(fault, swapoff, MADV_WILLNEED, UFFDIO_MOVE). MADV_FREE does not consult
the cache: it frees a whole PMD swap entry in place and only splits when
the advised range covers part of the PMD. Likewise, if any slot is still
backed by zswap's per-page store, PMD-order swap-in consumers split and
let the PTE path load the range page by page; an all-on-disk range can
still be read back as one PMD-sized folio.

The series is ordered so every consumer can handle PMD swap entries
before the swap-out producer starts installing them. The swap-out patch
is the last functional change.

Performance (measurements from v8):

  Measured with vm-scalability's case-swap-w-seq benchmark [1]. Four
  pinned workers repeatedly write a 6 GiB anonymous working set on a
  4 vCPU / 4 GiB guest, forcing the set out to swap and back in. Swap
  is an 8 GiB NOCOW raw virtio device (cache=none, aio=native), zswap is
  disabled, and THP enabled/defrag are both "always". The numbers below
  are medians of five interleaved runs per kernel after one warm-up run:

  Metric                          Baseline     Patched      Change
  Aggregate throughput            584.3 MiB/s  2408.9 MiB/s +312.2% (4.12x)
  Elapsed time                    85.43 s      20.72 s      -75.7%
  Major faults                    1,814,699    228,466      -87.4%
  Swap I/O rate                   1.02 GiB/s   4.10 GiB/s   +303.9%

  This swap-intensive synthetic workload measures the reduction in
  swap-fault and page-table overhead from preserving PMD mappings.
  For long-running workloads, I expect benefits from fewer TLB misses,
  less khugepaged work and retaining larger folios. I have not yet found
  a benchmark that captures those benefits well. PMD swap entries also
  move us closer to eliminating page-table deposits for anonymous THPs,
  which would save memory.

Intermediate patches and Sashiko:

  Earlier patches prepare consumers while reclaim still requests
  TTU_SPLIT_HUGE_PMD. PMD swap entries cannot reach those consumers until
  the swap-out producer is enabled. Concerns requiring live PMD swap
  entries before that patch describe an unreachable state. See [2].
  The v8 Sashiko report failed to apply and supplied no findings.

Notes on zswap:

  Native PMD-order zswap load/store is left for a follow-up.
  Alexandre Ghiti is currently working on this.
  This series can still preserve PMD swap entries while zswap is enabled:
  zswap stores the THP as order-0 entries, and PMD-order swap-in
  consumers split any range that has zswap entries before reading it.
  If zswap has written the whole range back to disk, or the swap cache
  still contains one PMD-sized folio, PMD-level handling can proceed.

[1] https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/wfg/vm-scalability.git/tree/case-swap-w-seq
[2] https://lore.kernel.org/all/282ef982-3e48-4283-9155-73a33fc1c4e8@linux.dev/

review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the s390 architecture's swap PMD layout, explaining that it is an RSTE with its own layout and requiring its own exclusive bit rather than borrowing from the PTE-format macro.
review_comments.raw_body:
Prepare for keeping a PMD-mapped anonymous THP mapped by a PMD across the
swap round-trip, which makes PG_anon_exclusive have to survive in a swap
PMD and not just in a swap PTE.

s390 is the one architecture where a swap PMD is not a swap PTE in
disguise: it is an RSTE with its own layout, converted to a fake PTE swap
entry for the common code. Give it its own exclusive bit rather than
borrowing the PTE-format macro, and document it in the RSTE swap layout,
where bit 52 was listed as unused.

 1 file changed, 18 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)

diff --git a/arch/s390/include/asm/pgtable.h b/arch/s390/include/asm/pgtable.h
index 2d5c2ab06de98..2c6b5205ee3bc 100644
--- a/arch/s390/include/asm/pgtable.h
+++ b/arch/s390/include/asm/pgtable.h
@@ -333,6 +333,7 @@ void setup_protection_map(void);
 /* Common bits in region and segment table entries, for swap entries */
 #define _RST_ENTRY_COMM		0x0010	/* Common-Region/Segment, marks swap entry */
 #define _RST_ENTRY_INVALID	0x0020	/* invalid region/segment table entry */
+#define _RST_ENTRY_SWP_EXCLUSIVE 0x0800	/* SW exclusive swap bit, see mk_swap_rste() */
 
 #define _CRST_ENTRIES	2048	/* number of region/segment table entries */
 #define _PAGE_ENTRIES	256	/* number of page table entries	*/
@@ -893,6 +894,21 @@ static inline pmd_t pmd_clear_soft_dirty(pmd_t pmd)
 }
 
 #ifdef CONFIG_ARCH_HAS_PMD_SOFTLEAVES
+static inline bool pmd_swp_exclusive(pmd_t pmd)
+{
+	return pmd_val(pmd) & _RST_ENTRY_SWP_EXCLUSIVE;
+}
+
+static inline pmd_t pmd_swp_mkexclusive(pmd_t pmd)
+{
+	return set_pmd_bit(pmd, __pgprot(_RST_ENTRY_SWP_EXCLUSIVE));
+}
+
+static inline pmd_t pmd_swp_clear_exclusive(pmd_t pmd)
+{
+	return clear_pmd_bit(pmd, __pgprot(_RST_ENTRY_SWP_EXCLUSIVE));
+}
+
 #define pmd_swp_soft_dirty(pmd)		pmd_soft_dirty(pmd)
 #define pmd_swp_mksoft_dirty(pmd)	pmd_mksoft_dirty(pmd)
 #define pmd_swp_clear_soft_dirty(pmd)	pmd_clear_soft_dirty(pmd)
@@ -1900,15 +1916,15 @@ static inline swp_entry_t __swp_entry(unsigned long type, unsigned long offset)
  * Bits 59 and 63 are used to indicate the swap entry. Bit 58 marks the rste
  * as invalid.
  * A swap entry is indicated by bit pattern (rste & 0x011) == 0x010
- * |			  offset			|Xtype |11TT|S0|
+ * |			  offset			|Etype |11TT|S0|
  * |0000000000111111111122222222223333333333444444444455|555555|5566|66|
  * |0123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901|234567|8901|23|
  *
  * Bits 0-51 store the offset.
+ * Bit 52 (E) is used to remember PG_anon_exclusive (_RST_ENTRY_SWP_EXCLUSIVE).
  * Bits 53-57 store the type.
  * Bit 62 (S) is used for softdirty tracking.
  * Bits 60-61 (TT) indicate the table type: 0x01 for REGION3 and 0x00 for SEGMENT.
- * Bit 52 (X) is unused.
  */
 
 #define __SWP_OFFSET_MASK_RSTE	((1UL << 52) - 1)

Prepare for keeping a PMD-mapped anonymous THP mapped by a PMD across the
swap round-trip, which makes PG_anon_exclusive have to survive in a swap

version_history.subject: [PATCH v2] x86/lib: Use REP MOVSB for large memcpy() on ERMS CPUs without FSRM

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch optimizes large memory copies on ERMS CPUs without FSRM by using the REP MOVSB instruction from 2048 bytes onwards, reducing execution time by up to 66.8%. The patch also folds memcpy_orig() into __memcpy() and makes adjustments for FSRM CPUs. Smaller copies continue to use a scalar loop for performance reasons.

review_comments.author: David Laight
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer David Laight noted that the patch does not handle misaligned copies of size 512 to 640 bytes correctly, which were slower than the scalar loop in v1, and requested raising the threshold from 512 to 2048 bytes.

Reviewer David Laight questioned the patch's assumption that REP MOVSB would always improve performance on ERMS CPUs, citing specific alignment issues on Zen and Intel CPUs, including a case where REP MOVSB is slower due to misalignment between source and destination buffers.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed,  4 Nov 2026 14:28:06 -0800
Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev> wrote:

---

Which cpu type was that?
Do I remember the older zen cpu falling back to byte copies?
I wonder if it is possibly to do a run-time patch of the constant.
In all the tests I've done on Intel cpu (going back to sandy bridge)
the only alignment that made any difference was 64 byte (32 on older cpu)
alignment of the destination buffer.

That could be 'for further study'.

There are some very bad alignment pairs on some cpu.
On zen5 if (IIRC) (src - dest) % PAGE_SIZE is between 1 and 127 then
the both setup and per-byte cost of REP MOSVB are significantly higher
(the byte alignment makes minimal difference throughout).
I don't remember finding anything similar on the Intel cpu I tested.
But it is probably not worth checking for them because the cost of the
comparison will be larger overall.

David

review_comments.author: Usama Arif (author)
review_comments.summary:
The author addressed a concern about the patch's applicability to specific CPU models by confirming that Zen 1 and Zen 2 do not have ERMS or FSRM, thus keeping the scalar loop, while Zen 3 onwards use REP MOVSB for every size.

Author acknowledges that using REP MOVSB for small copies might be beneficial but wants to prioritize the current usecase-driven approach from zstd/btrfs.

The author clarifies that the performance issue with REP MOVSB on misaligned copies between 512 and 640 bytes was due to specific alignment, not a general problem with using REP MOVSB at this threshold.

Author agrees that the current patch is acceptable, but suggests investigating further if a use case for smaller sizes can be found.
review_comments.raw_body:
I just checked, and Zen 1 and Zen 2 have neither ERMS nor FSRM, so
they keep the scalar loop. Zen 3 onwards has both, and FSRM already
uses REP MOVSB for every size.

---

It might be possible. But I wanted to keep the patch usecase driven.
The current usecase is coming from zstd/btrfs. If we find a usecase
where it might be faster for smaller copies, it might become worth
looking into then?

---

Also I should have been clearer in the changelog, by "misaligned copies of
512 to 640 bytes", I had tested a 513-byte copy with the source at page offset
1 and destination at 63, it took on average 62 ns with REP MOVSB versus
49 ns with scalar. I had done a couple of other tests at 640 bytes as well.

---

Yes, I agree.

Do you think this version of the patch seems acceptable?

I feel like we should only investigate for lower size if we can find a
usecase.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Kiryl Shutsemau questioned whether any RET in a replacement needs to be aligned, and suggested comparing Linus' layout which keeps the RET out of the replacement, potentially avoiding an ITS problem.

Reviewer noted that the RCX/RDX swap in the patch only saves one MOV on copies of 2K and up, and suggested an alternative implementation to replace the swap with a conditional jump based on ERMS feature

	RET

-	movq %rdi, %rax
-
